common_name: Moongold Apricot (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Apricot, Sungold Pollinizer Pair)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Moongold is self-unfruitful and must be planted with Sungold apricot nearby for pollination, since the two were bred as a matched pair.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, always alongside a Sungold apricot, since Moongold cannot pollinate itself and the two varieties were specifically bred and released together by the University of Minnesota as a compatible pollination pair for cold climates. The medium-sized, yellow-orange fruit has sweet, juicy flesh good for fresh eating, canning, and preserves, produced by a genuinely cold-hardy tree that extends apricot growing well into regions too harsh for most other varieties. As with most cold-hardy northern apricots, the tree's biggest challenge is not winter cold but early spring bloom, which can be damaged by a late frost even though the tree itself survives severe winter temperatures without difficulty; a site that avoids low-lying frost pockets helps protect the crop.

common_name: Sungold Apricot (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Apricot, Moongold Pollinizer Pair)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Sungold is self-unfruitful and must be planted with Moongold apricot nearby for pollination, since the two were bred as a matched pair.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, always alongside a Moongold apricot, since Sungold cannot pollinate itself and the two varieties were released together by the University of Minnesota specifically to pollinate one another in cold climates. The medium, golden-yellow fruit has sweet, tender flesh good for fresh eating and preserving, and the tree carries the same excellent cold hardiness as its pollination partner, allowing apricot production in regions well north of where most other varieties can survive winter. Because spring frost during the tree's early bloom is a greater practical risk than winter cold itself, site the pair away from low frost pockets and, where possible, in a slightly elevated or air-draining location to reduce frost damage to the flowers that determine the year's crop.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Harglow is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Harglow was bred at the Harrow research station in Ontario, Canada, valued for combining good cold hardiness with notably strong resistance to perennial canker, a bacterial disease that seriously damages many apricot trees in humid or variable climates. The small to medium, orange fruit has firm, richly flavored flesh with a good sweet-tart balance, excellent for fresh eating as well as preserving. The compact tree size makes it a practical fit for smaller home orchards, and its disease resistance gives it real staying power compared with more disease-prone apricot varieties in regions where canker and other bacterial issues are common. Thin fruit if a heavy crop sets, and prune to an open form for good air circulation, which further reduces disease pressure.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; extremely cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 2-6, though a second seedling apricot or Manchurian-type tree nearby improves fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Westcot was bred on the Canadian Prairies from Manchurian apricot stock specifically to survive the extreme winter cold of Saskatchewan and similar climates, extending apricot growing into regions far too harsh for standard European apricot varieties. The small, orange-yellow fruit is smaller and slightly tarter than familiar supermarket apricots but is genuinely good for fresh eating, drying, and preserves, and represents one of the few reliable ways prairie and northern growers can produce apricots at all. As with other extreme-hardy apricots, the tree itself easily survives severe winter cold, but early spring bloom remains vulnerable to late frost, so choose a planting site that avoids frost pockets and drains cold air away from the tree during bloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; extremely cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 2-6, and benefits from a second hardy apricot nearby for best fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Scout is another Saskatchewan-developed apricot bred from cold-hardy Manchurian apricot stock, part of a small group of extreme-hardy prairie apricot selections developed to give northern growers a genuine option for growing apricots where standard varieties cannot survive winter. Fruit is small to medium with orange skin and flesh, tarter and less refined than warm-climate apricots but entirely usable for fresh eating, drying, and preserves, and a genuine novelty for gardeners in short-season, harsh-winter climates. As with other prairie apricots, the tree's cold hardiness is exceptional, but flowers open early and remain vulnerable to spring frost, so site selection to avoid frost pockets matters more for the annual crop than winter survival does.
